title: The water cycle
summary: Follow a drop of water as it rises into the sky, makes a cloud, falls as rain, and starts all over again.
objective: Explain how water travels in a loop: evaporation, condensation, precipitation, and collection.

hook.prompt: You hang a wet towel outside in the sun. A few hours later, it's dry. Where did the water go?

options.text: Up into the air, where you can't see it
It disappeared forever
options.feedback: Water doesn't vanish. It changed into something you can't see, and it's still out there.

options.text: The sun burned it up
options.feedback: The sun warmed the water, but water can't burn. It went somewhere.

options.text: It all dripped onto the ground
options.feedback: A little might drip, but a towel in the sun dries even with no puddle underneath.

hook.explanation: The water turned into an invisible gas and floated into the air. That's the first step of a giant loop water travels around Earth.

bricks.title: The sun lifts water into the air
bricks.body: When the sun warms water in oceans, lakes, and puddles, some of it turns into **water vapor**: a gas, like air, that you can't see. The vapor floats up into the sky. This is called **evaporation**. The warmer the water, the faster it evaporates. That's why wet clothes dry faster on a hot, sunny day.

term.definition: When liquid water warms up and turns into invisible water vapor that rises into the air.

visual.alt: The sun shines on a lake, and dashed wavy arrows show invisible water vapor rising from the water into the sky.

bricks.prompt: After a rainstorm, there are two puddles the same size. Which one will dry up first?

options.text: The puddle in the sunny playground
The puddle in the shade under a big tree
options.feedback: The shade keeps that puddle cooler, so it evaporates more slowly.

options.text: They'll dry at exactly the same time
options.feedback: They're the same size, but not the same warmth. Warmer water evaporates faster.

bricks.explanation: The sun warms the playground puddle more, and warmer water evaporates faster.

bricks.prompt: Which of these shows water evaporating?

options.text: A wet swimsuit drying on a sunny fence
An ice cube turning into a little puddle
options.feedback: The ice changed, but it's still liquid water you can see. Evaporation is when water turns into invisible vapor and floats away.

options.text: Rain falling on a window
options.feedback: That's water coming down from the sky, not rising up into it.

options.text: Pouring water into a glass
options.feedback: The water is just moving from place to place. It's still liquid water you can see.

bricks.hint: Look for water that disappears into the air.
bricks.explanation: The sun warms the water in the swimsuit, so it turns into invisible vapor and rises into the air.

bricks.title: Cold turns vapor back into drops
bricks.body: When water vapor cools down, it turns back into tiny drops of liquid water. This is called **condensation**. You can see it on a cold glass of lemonade on a hot day: drops of water appear on the *outside* of the glass. High in the sky, the air is cold, so rising vapor condenses into billions of tiny drops or bits of ice. Together, they make a **cloud**.

term.definition: When water vapor cools and turns back into tiny drops of liquid water.

visual.alt: A cold glass of lemonade with ice cubes, with small drops of water stuck to the outside of the glass.

bricks.prompt: You take a cold can of juice outside on a hot day. Soon the outside of the can is wet. Where did that water come from?

options.text: Water vapor in the air cooled down on the cold can
Juice leaked out through the metal
options.feedback: The can has no holes, and the drops are plain water, not juice. The water came from outside the can.

options.text: The can is sweating, like people do
options.feedback: Cans can't sweat. The water came from the air around the can.

options.text: The cold made brand-new water appear
options.feedback: Cold can't make new water. It turned vapor that was already in the air into drops.

bricks.hint: What's floating in the air that you can't see?
bricks.explanation: The air holds invisible water vapor. When it touches the cold can, it cools and condenses into drops.

bricks.prompt: You can't see water vapor. So why can you see a cloud?

options.text: The vapor cooled into tiny drops of water or bits of ice
Clouds are made of smoke
options.feedback: Clouds are made of water. Smoke comes from fires.

options.text: When lots of vapor squeezes together, it turns white
options.feedback: Even lots of vapor stays invisible. It has to cool and condense into drops before you can see it.

bricks.hint: What happens to vapor when it gets cold?
bricks.explanation: High up, cold air makes the vapor condense into tiny drops or ice bits. Billions of them together are the cloud you see.

bricks.title: Rain falls, and the loop starts again
bricks.body: Inside a cloud, tiny drops bump together and grow. When they get too heavy to float, they fall. Water falling from clouds is **precipitation**: rain, or snow, sleet, and hail when it's cold. The water then gathers in oceans, lakes, and rivers, or soaks into the ground. That's **collection**. Then the sun warms it again, and the loop starts over. This loop is the **water cycle**.

term.definition: Water that falls from clouds: rain, snow, sleet, or hail.

visual.html:
Evaporation
water rises as vapor
→
Condensation
vapor makes clouds
↑
↓
Collection
water gathers in oceans, lakes, and rivers
←
Precipitation
rain or snow falls
visual.alt: A loop of four steps with arrows: evaporation, then condensation, then precipitation, then collection, and back to evaporation.

bricks.prompt: Tap every picture that shows precipitation.
bricks.hint: Look for water falling down from a cloud.
bricks.explanation: Rain and snow are both water falling from clouds, so both are precipitation. A cloud by itself is condensation, and vapor rising from the ocean is evaporation.

bricks.prompt: A drop of water starts in a lake. Put its trip around the water cycle in order.

items.text: The sun warms the lake, and the water evaporates
The invisible vapor rises high into the cold sky
The vapor condenses into tiny drops and makes a cloud
The drops grow heavy and fall as rain
The rain runs into a river that flows back to the lake

bricks.hint: Start with what the sun does to the lake.
bricks.explanation: Evaporation lifts the water, condensation makes the cloud, precipitation brings it down, and collection gathers it back in the lake.

challenge.prompt: Maya puts a little water in a plastic bag, seals it, and tapes it to a sunny window. Hours later, drops cover the inside of the bag and slide back down. What's happening?

visual.alt: A sealed plastic bag taped to a sunny window, with water at the bottom and small drops stuck to the inside near the top.

options.text: The water evaporates, condenses on the cooler plastic, and falls back down: a tiny water cycle
Rain from outside is leaking in through the window
options.feedback: The bag is sealed, so no water can get in. The drops came from the water already inside.

options.text: The sun is making new water inside the bag
options.feedback: No new water appears. The same water just changes: liquid, then vapor, then drops again.

options.text: The water is only evaporating, so the bag will soon be dry
options.feedback: Evaporation starts it, but the vapor can't escape a sealed bag. It condenses into drops that fall back down.

challenge.hint: Follow the water: what does the sun do to it, and what happens when the vapor touches the plastic?
challenge.explanation: The sun warms the water and it evaporates. The vapor cools on the plastic and condenses. Heavy drops fall. Same water, going round and round.

takeaways: The sun warms water, and it evaporates into invisible water vapor.
When vapor cools, it condenses into tiny drops that make clouds.
Heavy drops fall as precipitation, collect in oceans, lakes, and rivers, and the loop starts again.
